item.title: “Once, monks, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, monks, the quail, while being carried off by the hawk, lamented: ‘This is…
item.description:
“Once, monks, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, monks, the quail, while being carried off by the hawk, lamented: ‘This is my misfortune! This is my lack of merit! For I wandered outside my own proper range, into the domain of others. If I had kept to my own proper range, my ancestral territory, this hawk would not have been a match for me in battle.’ - ‘What, quail, is your own proper range, your ancestral territory?’ - ‘A field plowed with a plow.’ Then, monks, the hawk, not boasting of its own strength, not pressing its own strength, released the quail and said: ‘Go, quail. Even after going there, I will not let you go.’ Then, monks, the quail went to a field plowed with a plow, climbed onto a large clod of earth, stood on it, and said to the hawk: ‘Come at me, hawk! Come at me, hawk!’ Then the hawk, boasting of its own strength, pressing its own strength, folding both wings, suddenly swooped down on the quail. When the quail knew: ‘This hawk is swooping down hard on me,’ it hid behind that clod of earth. Then, monks, the hawk shattered its own breast. So too, monks, for one who wanders outside his own proper range, into the domain of others. Therefore, monks, do not wander outside your own proper range, into the domain of others. For one who wanders outside his proper range, into the domain of others, Māra gains an opportunity, Māra gains an object.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.6

item.title: “Monks, there is no form that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain forever. There is no feeling … perception ……
item.description:
“Monks, there is no form that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain forever. There is no feeling … perception … formation … consciousness that is permanent, everlasting, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain forever.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.98

item.title: “Monks, just as a great tree, having its roots that extend downward and laterally, all those roots convey the sap upwards — that great tree,…
item.description:
“Monks, just as a great tree, having its roots that extend downward and laterally, all those roots convey the sap upwards — that great tree, being nourished and sustained in such a way, would stand for a long time. So too, monks, one who dwells seeing gratification in things that are clung to — craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging arises … Thus the origination of this whole mass of suffering. Monks, just as a great tree, and a man comes with a shovel and a basket. He cuts the tree’s roots … He digs a trench … he pulls out the rootlets … or he burns the tree and scatters the ashes in a strong stream of water. That great tree, with its roots cut, made like a palm stump, cannot be reborn, cannot arise again in the future. So too, monks, one who dwells seeing peril in things that are clung to — craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, clinging ceases … Thus the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.56

item.title: “Monks, if a monk, while attending to some sign and giving attention to it, has evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, ill-will, and delusion arise.…
item.description:
“Monks, if a monk, while attending to some sign and giving attention to it, has evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, ill-will, and delusion arise. That monk attends to a different sign connected with what is wholesome, not that sign. Those evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, ill-will, and delusion are abandoned and subside. With their abandonment, the mind becomes steadied, settled, unified, and concentrated.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 20 – Vitakkasaṇṭhānasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And how, monks, is a monk ‘one who has learned’? He has destroyed evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful, producing…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is a monk ‘one who has learned’? He has destroyed evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful, producing painful results, leading to future birth, aging, and death. Thus, monks, a monk is ‘one who has learned.’”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 39 – Mahāhatthipadopamasutta

item.title: “Sāriputta, while a noble disciple attains and dwells in the rapture born of seclusion, during that time five things do not occur for him: pain…
item.description:
“Sāriputta, while a noble disciple attains and dwells in the rapture born of seclusion, during that time five things do not occur for him: pain and grief connected with sensuality do not occur; pleasure and joy connected with sensuality do not occur; pain and grief connected with the unwholesome do not occur; pleasure and joy connected with the unwholesome do not occur; pain and grief connected with the wholesome do not occur. Sāriputta, while a noble disciple attains and dwells in the rapture born of seclusion, during that time these five things do not occur for him.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.176
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, what one intends, what one plans, and what one has a tendency towards — that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When…
item.description:
“Monks, what one intends, what one plans, and what one has a tendency towards — that becomes a basis for the establishment of consciousness. When there is a basis, there is an establishment of consciousness. When consciousness is established and grows, there is the descent of name-and-form. With name-and-form as condition, the six sense-bases; with the six sense-bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling … craving … clinging … existence … birth; aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.39
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does not delight in…
item.description:
“Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does not delight in those forms, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then that monk is called one who has not swallowed Māra’s hook, who has broken the hook, destroyed the hook, who has not fallen into misfortune, into calamity, not subject to the Evil One’s will. There are sounds … odors … tastes … touches … phenomena cognizable by the mind … If a monk does not delight in those phenomena, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then that monk is called one who has not swallowed Māra’s hook, who has broken the hook, destroyed the hook, who has not fallen into misfortune, into calamity, not subject to the Evil One’s will.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.230

item.title: “Monks, it is because of not realizing, not penetrating four things that you and I have wandered for such a long time in this cycle…
item.description:
“Monks, it is because of not realizing, not penetrating four things that you and I have wandered for such a long time in this cycle of birth and death. What four? Monks, because of not realizing, not penetrating noble virtue, you and I have wandered for such a long time in this cycle of birth and death. Monks, because of not realizing, not penetrating noble concentration … noble wisdom … noble liberation, you and I have wandered for such a long time in this cycle of birth and death.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 16 – Mahāparinibbānasutta

item.title: “And how, monks, is a monk called a ‘noble one’? He has made distant evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful,…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is a monk called a ‘noble one’? He has made distant evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful, producing painful results, leading to future birth, aging, and death. Thus, monks, a monk is called a noble one.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 39 – Mahāhatthipadopamasutta
